question: Does Metformin reduce cardiovascular mortality in patients with chronic kidney disease?
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metformin is the first-line pharmacotherapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus, but concerns regarding lactic acidosis historically limited its use in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 25,148 diabetic patients with CKD stages 1-4. Cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality, and incidence of lactic acidosis were analyzed over a 5-year follow-up period.
RESULTS: Metformin users with stage 3 CKD (eGFR 30-59 mL/min/1.73 m2) exhibited a 22% lower risk of cardiovascular mortality (adjusted HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.91) and a 19% reduction in all-cause mortality compared with non-users. Rates of lactic acidosis did not differ significantly between metformin users and non-users across stage 1 to stage 3b CKD (0.12 vs 0.09 per 1000 person-years, p=0.45).
CONCLUSIONS: Metformin use is associated with reduced cardiovascular and all-cause mortality in diabetic patients with stage 1-3b CKD without a significant elevation in lactic acidosis risk.
golden_answer: Yes. Clinical evidence shows that Metformin is associated with a 22% reduction in cardiovascular mortality in diabetic patients with CKD stages 1-3b, without significantly increasing the risk of lactic acidosis.

question: What is the recommended dose adjustment for Apixaban in patients with severe renal impairment?
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) undergo variable renal elimination. Apixaban is 27% renally cleared, making it a common choice in renal impairment.
METHODS: Pharmacokinetic profiles and bleeding outcomes from the ARISTOTLE trial and post-marketing surveillance were reviewed for patients with creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min.
RESULTS: Standard dosing is 5 mg twice daily. Dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily is recommended if patients meet at least two of the following criteria: age >= 80 years, body weight <= 60 kg, or serum creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL (133 micromol/L). In patients on chronic hemodialysis without these criteria, 5 mg twice daily maintains therapeutic levels, whereas meeting two criteria warrants 2.5 mg twice daily.
CONCLUSIONS: Dose adjustment of apixaban is guided by the ABC criteria (Age, Body weight, Creatinine) rather than isolated eGFR cutoff alone.
golden_answer: Apixaban standard dosing is 5 mg twice daily, reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily if the patient meets at least two of the following: age >= 80 years, weight <= 60 kg, or serum creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL.

question: Do preoperative statins reduce the incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation after coronary artery bypass grafting?
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) occurs in 20-40% of patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and is associated with increased stroke risk and hospital stay.
METHODS: A double-blind, randomized controlled trial evaluated 1,922 patients assigned to receive atorvastatin (20 mg/day) or placebo starting 7 days prior to scheduled elective on-pump CABG.
RESULTS: The incidence of POAF was 21.1% in the atorvastatin group compared to 28.6% in the placebo group (odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.53-0.84, p < 0.001). Preoperative C-reactive protein elevation was significantly attenuated in the statin group.
CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative statin therapy significantly decreases the incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation in patients undergoing CABG.
golden_answer: Yes. Preoperative statin administration significantly decreases the incidence of postoperative atrial fibrillation following CABG (OR 0.67).

question: Does routine hydroxychloroquine administration improve clinical recovery in hospitalized COVID-19 patients?
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hydroxychloroquine was hypothesized to exert antiviral and anti-inflammatory effects in severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 infection.
METHODS: In the RECOVERY trial, 1,561 hospitalized COVID-19 patients were randomized to hydroxychloroquine and 3,155 to usual standard care.
RESULTS: 28-day mortality was 27.0% in the hydroxychloroquine group and 25.0% in the usual care group (rate ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.97-1.23, p=0.15). Patients in the hydroxychloroquine group had a longer median duration of hospital stay (16 vs 13 days) and a higher frequency of invasive mechanical ventilation or death (30.7% vs 26.9%).
CONCLUSIONS: In hospitalized patients with COVID-19, hydroxychloroquine did not result in lower 28-day mortality or improved clinical outcomes compared with standard of care.
golden_answer: No. Large-scale randomized trials (such as RECOVERY) demonstrated that hydroxychloroquine did not improve 28-day mortality or clinical recovery in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

question: What is essential hypertension?
abstract: Essential hypertension (primary hypertension) is high blood pressure with no identifiable secondary cause. It accounts for approximately 90-95% of all adult cases of hypertension and is managed with lifestyle modification and first-line antihypertensive agents such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, CCBs, or thiazide diuretics.
golden_answer: Essential (primary) hypertension is chronic high blood pressure that has no identifiable secondary cause, accounting for 90-95% of adult hypertension cases.

question: In a diabetic patient with eGFR of 35 mL/min and a history of atrial fibrillation, can Metformin and Apixaban be co-administered safely?
abstract: Metformin can be continued in CKD stage 3a/3b with close renal monitoring and eGFR >= 30 mL/min. Apixaban requires dose reduction to 2.5 mg BID if creatinine is >= 1.5 mg/dL along with age >= 80 or weight <= 60 kg. No direct pharmacokinetic drug-drug interaction exists between metformin (organic cation transporter substrate) and apixaban (CYP3A4/P-gp substrate).
golden_answer: Yes, Metformin and Apixaban can be co-administered in patients with eGFR of 35 mL/min, provided Metformin is kept under 1000 mg/day with frequent renal monitoring, and Apixaban dose is adjusted if age >= 80 or weight <= 60 kg.
